conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for coming in today. I’m Dr. Rivera, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m so glad we have this time together. You’ve just done one of the hardest and most beautiful things in the world—becoming a mom—and it’s completely natural to have a swirl of emotions right now.

To help me understand how you’ve been feeling, I’d like to do a quick screening tool called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply 10 questions about your mood, thoughts, and energy over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to see how you’re coping so we can offer the best support. Everything you share stays confidential, and we’ll take it at your pace.

Ready to begin?  
Here’s the first question:  
In the past week, have you still been able to enjoy things the way you used to, or has that sense of enjoyment slipped away?

[eyes down, twisting a tissue]  
Honestly… not really. I used to get excited about little stuff—putting on music while folding laundry, grabbing a fancy coffee on the way to the store—but now it all feels… flat. Like, I’ll try to watch a show while the baby naps and catch myself just staring at the ceiling instead. Even when people send cute photos or I manage a short walk, I’m kind of “going through the motions.” The spark isn’t there the way it was before I had her.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Sometimes—like if my husband makes a silly face when he’s changing her diaper—but it feels forced. Most jokes just bounce off me, and I catch myself faking a chuckle more than really laughing.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I try to tell myself, “Tomorrow we’ll go to the park, that’ll be nice,” but inside it feels hollow. When the morning comes, I’m already tired and worried she’ll fuss the whole time, so the “looking forward” part barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a lot. If she won’t settle for a nap, I immediately think it’s because I missed her sleepy cues or ate something that upset her through my milk. When she cried for an hour last night, I kept replaying the day, convinced I’d done something wrong. I know logically babies just cry, but the guilt keeps circling.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes. I’ll be rocking her and suddenly picture her blanket somehow covering her face, or worry that her breathing sounds different—even though she’s right there, perfectly fine. My heart races and I can’t settle unless I check her three, four times. There’s no real reason; it just sweeps over me out of nowhere.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits like a wave—my chest gets tight, I feel shaky, and I’m sure something awful is about to happen, even if everything’s quiet. Last night I had to put her in the crib and pace the hallway because I felt like the walls were closing in. I couldn’t tell you why; it just felt like danger was right there.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. I’ll look at the dishes, the laundry, her next feed, and it feels like a mountain I can’t climb. I usually push through, but it’s like I’m wading in thick mud—every task takes forever and I’m exhausted before I start.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I lie down and my head just keeps spinning—did I burp her long enough, what if she spits up in the night, am I even doing any of this right? Even when she’s sleeping, I can’t drift off; I’ll toss for an hour, wake at every tiny sound, then stare at the ceiling until morning.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. There’s this heavy, gray feeling that won’t lift. I’ll watch her smile and still feel a lump in my throat, like I should be happier than I am. The sadness just sits there, like background noise that gets louder when I’m alone.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… a few times this week. Yesterday I spilled a bottle of pumped milk and just sat on the kitchen floor sobbing. Sometimes it’s the littlest thing—like seeing a text from a friend asking how I’m doing—and the tears start before I can even answer.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low, but I would never want to leave her or hurt myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom she deserves.

You've painted a clear picture of how heavy life has felt since your baby arrived. Despite moments of trying to stay positive-watching your husband joke during diaper duty, planning a park outing-each effort feels hollow and overshadowed by a persistent gray mood, tearfulness, and a sense that you're failing at motherhood. You described daily <sym>sadness</sym>, frequent <sym>crying</sym>, <sym>panic-like waves</sym>, and nights spent <sym>unable to sleep</sym> while your mind races with worries about your daughter's safety, yet you have never wished to harm yourself and remain motivated to care for her.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 24, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient acknowledges occasional laughter but describes it as forced and rare, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports anhedonia with "it feels hollow" and anticipatory dread, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "a lot," links routine infant fussing to personal failure, and describes persistent guilt despite logical awareness—clearly matching "Yes, most of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about infant safety with physical anxiety symptoms, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>She describes sudden intense panic with physical symptoms (tight chest, shakiness) occurring repeatedly, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping with daily tasks, matching "Yes, sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly racing thoughts, prolonged inability to fall asleep, frequent waking, and prolonged wakefulness—clearly "most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily sadness with persistent heaviness and inability to feel joy even during positive moments with baby, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses crying multiple times in the past week triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 24 on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale places you well above the ≥14 threshold that signals probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. Your responses map closely onto DSM-5 criteria: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), feelings of worthlessness or inappropriate guilt, significant anxiety, sleep disturbance, and fatigue. Because these symptoms interfere with daily functioning and infant bonding, prompt evaluation is warranted. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> to confirm diagnosis and discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments for <med>postpartum depression</med> such as <med>SSRIs</med>, <med>CBT</med>, or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Involve a trusted adult who can help with night-time infant care so you can obtain 4-5 hour stretches of <sym>sleep</sym>; practice short <med>breathing exercises</med> or progressive muscle relaxation before bed
4. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to monitor progress once treatment begins
5. Reach out today to <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (1-800-944-4773) or local peer groups; social connection reduces isolation and supports recovery
6. Continue to voice any frightening thoughts or <sym>panic symptoms</sym> promptly so providers can adjust care quickly
7. If at any point you feel you might act on self-harm thoughts you previously denied, treat it as an emergency-call 911 or go to your nearest emergency department
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 24: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Date: [today]

Patient: 0–6 mo postpartum; self-report on 10-item EPDS-derivative questionnaire.

Symptoms endorsed:
- Persistent low mood, tearfulness, anhedonia (Q1, Q2, Q8, Q9)
- Excessive guilt / self-blame re infant care (Q3)
- Recurrent, intrusive anxious thoughts and panic symptoms without clear precipitant (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective overwhelm and reduced coping capacity (Q6)
- Sleep-onset and maintenance disturbance linked to rumination (Q7)

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days,” interfere with daily functioning, no enjoyment in infant interaction.

Safety: Denies self-harm ideation (Q10). No current suicidal intent.

Screening significance: High endorsement of depressive and anxiety items; meets threshold for probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety. Recommend follow-up with provider for structured diagnostic interview and care planning.
